draft.title: Cities and climate change
card: The urban heat island effect is when a city is hotter than the land around it. Dark roads and roofs soak up heat, and buildings and paving leave few plants to cool the air.
Climate change is making the world warmer, so it can make heat islands worse. Hot days in a city can become hotter and more dangerous for people.
Cities can adapt, which means changing to cope with a new problem. Street trees and shade cool the air. Light-coloured cool roofs reflect heat instead of soaking it up.
Climate change can also bring heavier rain. Flood-safe planning, such as keeping homes away from flood-prone land and leaving open ground to soak up water, lowers the risk.
draft.remember: Cities trap heat, and climate change can add to it. Trees, shade, cool roofs and flood-safe planning help cities adapt.

a.q: Why can the centre of a city be hotter than farmland nearby?
opts: Dark roads and roofs soak up heat and few plants cool it
Cities sit closer to the sun than farmland does
Farmland is covered in dark surfaces that reflect heat away
People in a city give off more heat than machines do
a.why: Dark surfaces take in heat and there are fewer plants to cool the air, so the city heats up. Being close to the sun is not the reason, because the city and the farmland are about the same distance from it.
a.clue: Think about what the ground is covered with.

b.q: A council in Melbourne wants to cool a hot shopping street. Which action fits the urban heat island effect best?
opts: Plant street trees and add shade over the footpath
Widen the road and lay darker asphalt
Build more car parks with open, unshaded surfaces
Remove awnings so that more sun reaches the street
b.why: Trees and shade cool the air and block the sun, which reduces heat in the street. Darker asphalt soaks up more heat, so it would make the heat island effect worse.
b.clue: Which choice adds cooling and shade instead of heat-soaking surfaces?

a.best: Dark roads and roofs soak up heat and few plants cool it

b.best: Plant street trees and add shade over the footpath

problems.detail: The stem asks which action 'fits the urban heat island effect best', but darker asphalt and unshaded car parks would also 'fit' it by making it worse. The stem should ask which action would best reduce the heat island effect.
The clue 'Which choice adds cooling and shade instead of heat-soaking surfaces?' repeats the word 'shade' from the right option, so it gives the answer away.
